answer: Each agent must lock a unique stake in a shared registry before it can submit work, and disputes trigger random audits that slash the stake when evidence shows copied identities or collusion. This makes a Sybil swarm costly: splitting one actor into many agents requires funding each lock, while hiding coordination risks losing them all. An atlas of claims can reveal reused credentials; at the nadir, an attacker must either pay for many independent stakes or limit the swarm’s influence. Basalt-hard deposits make identities expensive to fake.
